name: KPV
summary: A three-amino-acid fragment of the hormone alpha-MSH, used for gut and skin inflammation on the strength of cell and animal studies; never tested in people.
what_it_is: KPV is a tiny peptide made of three amino acids (lysine, proline and valine) that matches the tail end of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH). In cell and rodent studies it dampened inflammatory signaling, possibly by blocking a pathway called NF-kB, but FDA says its molecular targets are still unknown. It has never been studied in humans, and in lab tests it crossed intact human skin poorly unless the skin barrier was broken.

evidence.why: FDA's 2026 review found only cell and rodent studies and no human data of any kind.

status_us.label: Not approved; FDA compounding decision pending
status_us.note: FDA took KPV off its Category 2 safety-risk list in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn. FDA staff advised against allowing it in compounding, but its advisory committee voted 8 to 6 (1 abstention) in favor on July 23, 2026; until FDA finishes rulemaking it is not on the list pharmacies may compound from, and an interim access policy has been under White House review since October 14, 2026.

benefits.claim: Reduced inflammatory signaling in human gut-lining cells and immune cells in lab studies
Anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in rodent models, including corneal wounds

risks.risk: No human safety data for any route, and no animal toxicity studies were found
Peptides can clump and trigger immune reactions (immunogenicity); FDA found too little data to rule this out
Available material is poorly characterized, with impurities and microbial testing not documented

avoid_if: Using it in place of proven treatment for a diagnosed condition such as inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, eczema or a chronic wound

before: General health check (blood count and metabolic panel)
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists because KPV has never been studied in people.

studies.title: FDA Briefing Document for KPV-Related Bulk Drug Substances (KPV (free base) and KPV acetate)
studies.people: Cell and rodent studies; no human data
studies.finding: FDA found no human data, no toxicity studies and poorly characterized material, and proposed not adding KPV to the 503A compounding list.

studies.title: Pept1-Mediated Tripeptide KPV Uptake Reduces Intestinal Inflammation
studies.people: Human intestinal and immune cell lines (as summarized by FDA)
studies.finding: A gut transporter called PepT1 carried KPV into cells, where it reduced inflammatory signaling.

ask_your_clinician: What proven treatments exist for my gut or skin symptoms, and have I tried them?
Should my inflammation be measured (for example CRP or fecal calprotectin) before I consider anything experimental?
What are the risks of using an unregulated product that has never been tested in people?

notes_for_editor: Seed record's status ('removed from restricted list, awaiting review') is now superseded: the advisory committee voted 8-6-1 for KPV on July 23, 2026, but FDA has made no decision and no rule has been proposed; an interim access policy is pending at OIRA, so status could change soon. The seed's mouse colitis study (Kannengiesser 2008) and the animal arm of Dalmasso 2008 could not be opened this session, so the gut benefit is limited to the cell findings FDA describes; the colitis studies should be added after checking them. Note the nomination FDA reviewed was for topical cream or gel for wounds and skin inflammation, not gut use.
